card.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model and its Limitations

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Rutherford's α-scattering experiment (1909–1911) on ~4 × 10⁻⁵ cm gold foil destroyed Thomson's pudding model: 99.86% of α-particles passed straight through (the atom is mostly empty space) while ~1 in 20,000 deflected >90° or bounced back — proof of a tiny (10⁻¹⁵ m), heavy, positive **nucleus** carrying nearly all the mass, with electrons revolving around it under Coulomb attraction.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) (scattering law) - r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) (distance of closest approach) - Nuclear radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m; atomic radius ~10⁻¹⁰ m

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Scattering source:** deflection comes from Coulomb **repulsion** between the positive α-particle and the positive nucleus — not from electron collisions (electrons are too light).  ·  **Atomic radius vs nuclear radius:** 10⁻¹⁰ m vs 10⁻¹⁵ m — the nucleus is 100,000× smaller in linear size but carries ~100% of the mass.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The atom consists of a tiny, heavy, positively charged nucleus around which electrons revolve."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***1 in 20,000 back-scattered*** — like a shell bouncing off tissue paper: the only explanation is a concentrated positive mass.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: No verified PYQ; NEB-style practice (experiment + conclusions 3–5m, limitations 3m).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Experiment That Found the Nucleus Thomson's plum-pudding model (1904) pictured the atom as diffuse positive charge with embedded electrons. Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden (1909–1911) fired α-particles (He²⁺, ~5.5 MeV) at gold foil ~4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick and got a result the pudding model could not survive: a few α-particles bounced straight back. The atom has a **nucleus**.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The set-up (state the four parts) 1. **α-source:** radium in a lead block with a collimator → narrow α-beam. 2. **Target:** gold foil ~4 × 10⁻⁵ cm (≈1000 atoms thick) — gold can be beaten very thin and has a heavy nucleus (Z = 79). 3. **Detector:** rotatable ZnS screen viewed through a microscope — each α-hit gives a scintillation. 4.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "PASS-THROUGH → empty; BOUNCE → nucleus; the two observations carry the whole answer."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): State the observations of Rutherford's α-scattering experiment and the conclusions drawn from each.** — (1) ~99.86% of α-particles passed straight through → the atom is mostly empty space. (2) ~1 in 20,000 deflected by >90°, a few bouncing back → a tiny, heavy, positively charged nucleus holds nearly all the mass.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Always pair the 10⁻¹⁵/10⁻¹⁰ m radii — the size contrast is a standing 1-mark item.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Observation → conclusion mapping** — each observation earns its conclusion; NEB marks the pairs, not the story.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: α-scattering on gold: 99.86% pass through (empty space); ~1/20,000 deflect >90° (tiny heavy positive nucleus). Limitations: stability (spiral in 10⁻⁸ s), continuous vs line spectra, no shells, no quantisation.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Rutherford called it "the most incredible event of my life" — as if firing a shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Bohr (Topic 14):** Bohr fixes exactly the two failures — stability and line spectra — by adding quantisation. - **To atomic number (Topic 24):** Moseley's X-ray work turned Rutherford's nuclear charge into Z. - **To nuclear chemistry:** the nucleus Rutherford found later yields the proton (1919) and neutron (1932).  ·  ## 4.
